Synopsis: Ted Rall wrote an LA Times article describing being handcuffed for jaywalking 14 years ago. LAPD contacts Nicholas Golderg at LA Times claiming that he wasn't handcuffed and provides a tape. The tape is fishy, so the LA Times asks the LAPD if it has been modified. The LAPD says no, so Nicholas Goldberg fires Ted Rall, claiming that the LAPD tape doesn't prove that he was handcuffed.

It looks like someone in the LAPPL police union went and found the tape and gave it to the LA Times without any authorization to do so and with the intent of getting Ted Rall fired. That person was a government employee and the target was a US citizen that was directly "harmed" as a result. Case law is clear: Rall's civil rights were violated by whoever did that.

That would be the situation even if the tape successfully made the case that Ted Rall had lied in an editorial that he wrote about being ticketed for jaywalking years ago, but the funny thing is that the tape actually wound up corroborating Rall's story and making Goldberg, look stupid for believing the LAPD's claims without checking them out.

The tapes contained three stops, with Ted Rall's stop being the middle one. In the first and third stops, the officer's voice can clearly be heard, but something was done in the middle stop where you couldn't hear much of anything, which was fishy. Running it through hiss reduction and cranking up human voice frequencies (I used cooledit pro.. it doesn't take an audio engineer to do basic poking around in poor audio recordings) reveals a crowd in the background and a woman's voice saying "Take off his handcuffs", so it actually looks like Rall was telling the truth about being handcuffed for a jaywalking stop 14 years ago.
